t.3.30.1: Then Śūrpaṇakhā, seeing the fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds slain by Rāma alone,
t.3.30.2: Seeing Dūṣaṇa and Khara, and Triśiras as well, slain in battle, she, like a rain-cloud, once again let out a mighty roar.
t.3.30.3: Having seen the deed accomplished by Rāma, one exceedingly difficult for others to perform, she, deeply agitated, went to Laṅkā, which was protected by Rāvaṇa.
t.3.30.4: She saw Rāvaṇa of blazing splendor at the top of his aerial palace, seated surrounded by his ministers like Vāsava surrounded by the Maruts.
t.3.30.5: Him, seated on a supreme golden throne bright as the sun, like a mighty fire blazing upon a golden altar.
t.3.30.6: He was a hero invincible in battle by the gods, gandharvas and spirits, and by the great-souled sages, like Antaka, Death himself, with his mouth gaping wide.
t.3.30.7: Him who bore wounds dealt by the vajra and the thunderbolt in the battles between the Devas and the Asuras, his chest marked with scars furrowed by the tips of Airāvata's tusks.
t.3.30.8: Twenty-armed Daśagrīva, splendid in his attire, broad-chested and heroic, marked with the signs of royalty.
t.3.30.9: She saw him gleaming like glossy beryl, wearing earrings of refined gold, with fine arms, white teeth and a huge mouth, towering like a mountain.
t.3.30.10: Him whose limbs had been struck hundreds of times in battle with the gods by the blows of Viṣṇu's discus, and likewise by all the weapons of the gods.
t.3.30.11: Him who stirs up the unshakable oceans, swift in action, the hurler of mountain peaks and the crusher of the gods.
t.3.30.13: He who went to the city of Bhogavatī, vanquished Vāsuki, and, having vanquished Takṣaka, carried off his beloved wife.
t.3.30.12: Him, the destroyer of the sacred laws, the violator of other men's wives, the wielder of every divine weapon, ever the obstructer of sacrifices.
t.3.30.14: He who, having gone to Mount Kailāsa and conquered Naravāhana, carried off his aerial chariot Puṣpaka, which moves wherever one wishes.
t.3.30.15: He who, mighty and in his wrath, lays waste the divine Caitraratha grove, the lotus lake, the Nandana grove, and the gardens of the gods.
t.3.30.16: He who, resembling a mountain peak, holds back with his two arms the illustrious Moon and Sun, those scorchers of foes, as they rise.
t.3.30.17: He who of old, steadfast, after practicing austerities in the great forest for ten thousand years, offered up his heads to Svayambhū.
t.3.30.19: He, the mighty one, who at the sacrifices destroys the holy soma pressed with mantras by the twice-born, as it stands in the havirdhāna sheds.
t.3.30.18: He is the one who, in battle, is free from fear of death at the hands of gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, birds and serpents, except from a human being.
t.3.30.21: The rākṣasī saw her cruel and mighty brother, the lord of the rākṣasas, illustrious, the delight of the Paulastya race, clad in divine garments and ornaments and adorned with heavenly garlands.
t.3.30.20: Rāvaṇa, cruel despoiler of duly performed sacrifices, slayer of brahmins, of wicked conduct, harsh and pitiless, intent on the harm of creatures, who brings terror to all beings throughout all the worlds.
t.3.30.22: Śūrpaṇakhā, who had once roamed without fear but had been disfigured by the great-souled one, now stupefied by fear and bewilderment, displayed herself and spoke exceedingly harsh words to him whose large eyes were blazing.
